title: Looking for a word
subtitle: School · Monday, 11:40 AM
focus: A pause can be part of finding the thought.

scenes.title: The word that arrives first

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: On Monday, Jules and I meet Minh in the library. Our project has changed from a map of meaningful places into a collection of short recordings about them.

lines.speaker: Minh
lines.text: What about recording dinner at your place? Just the sounds, or a little conversation. It sounded like a good evening.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: I like the idea, but I have not asked Mom. I imagine setting a microphone beside her bowl and announcing that our evening is now material for a class.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: The word that comes first is ngại. I know English. I also know that “shy” is not quite what I mean here. I am reluctant to put her on the spot.

lines.speaker: Jules
lines.text: We don't have to use it. What are you thinking?

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: There is enough space to answer, if I let myself use it. Minh slides the project notes toward me and waits.

scenes.prompt: How do you explain the hesitation?

note.title: Available words, particular meanings
note.text: For this fictional An, ngại arrives before a satisfying English phrasing. Its meaning depends on context. The scene represents one experience of searching for a word; it does not imply that bilingual people are generally less fluent or always translate internally.

choices.label: “I’m shy about asking her.”
choices.detail: Use the word you have right now.
choices.reflection: The short translation got the conversation moving. A follow-up helped distinguish reluctance from shyness.

reaction.speaker: Minh
reaction.text: Would it help if I asked her? I can write a message explaining the assignment.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Maybe. But it isn't really that I'm shy. I don't want her to feel she has to say yes because it is for my class.”

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Then let's make it easy to say no. We can have another idea ready before you ask.

choices.label: “I don’t want her to feel put on the spot.”
choices.detail: Describe the situation instead of finding one word.
choices.reflection: You made the concern actionable. Some of the feeling stayed outside the sentence.

reaction.speaker: Minh
reaction.text: That makes sense. We can tell her exactly what we'd record and let her decide later, away from us.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: The sentence does not contain every shade of what I feel. It does give us something useful to do. We write “ask first, no deadline for her answer” in the notes.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: And we can record the walk to campus if she doesn't want to. That is a place too.

choices.label: “I’m thinking of ngại. Here, I mean reluctant to impose.”
choices.detail: Keep the Vietnamese word and unpack your meaning.
choices.reflection: You let your friends hear the word behind the pause. Explaining it used some of your limited meeting time.

reaction.speaker: Minh
reaction.text: I use that word too, but I might have said “awkward” here. Is it more about asking her, or about recording home?

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Both, I think.” Even sharing a word does not mean Minh can read my mind. The question helps me separate the two concerns.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Let's leave room for both. We have ten minutes left, so maybe we choose a backup idea now and revisit the recording later.

scenes.title: One conversation, two languages

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: We start testing the recorder. I keep tapping the microphone instead of the record button. Minh reaches across the table to point out the tiny red circle.

lines.speaker: Minh
lines.text: Từ từ thôi, có ai đuổi đâu.
lines.translation: Slow down. No one's chasing you.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: I laugh before I think about which language the joke is in. Minh has the same amused expression my cousin gets when I rush through a task.

lines.speaker: Jules
lines.text: Wait, what did I miss? Is the recorder broken?

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: Nothing about the switch was planned. Still, Jules missed a piece of a conversation they are part of. I can make room without treating the Vietnamese as a mistake.

scenes.prompt: How do you bring Jules into the moment?

note.title: Switching and including
note.text: Language switching can serve humor, closeness, emphasis, or practical communication. Here it happens between two friends who share Vietnamese. Inclusion is a separate choice: a short bridge can invite Jules in without framing either language as unwelcome.

choices.label: “Minh said, ‘No one’s chasing you.’ I’m rushing.”
choices.detail: Share the image and why it was funny.
choices.reflection: You kept the joke's image and connected it to the situation.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Oh, absolutely. You look like that button has a deadline.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: Now all three of us are laughing. I press the right button, wait one second, and announce a very serious microphone test.

reaction.speaker: Minh
reaction.text: Perfect. We have recorded ourselves making fun of the recording process. Very experimental.

choices.label: “Just reminding me to slow down. The recorder’s fine.”
choices.detail: Give the part Jules needs to keep working.
choices.reflection: You cleared up the practical confusion quickly. The exact joke stayed between you and Minh.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Good. For a second I thought we'd have to borrow another one. Okay, let me try the headphones.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: We move on. I notice that Jules has the useful information, even if they do not have the exact joke. That can be enough for this moment.

reaction.speaker: Minh
reaction.text: Start whenever you're ready. Slowly, if possible.

choices.label: “It was a joke about me rushing. Minh, want to translate it?”
choices.reflection: You invited Minh to carry their own joke across. Translation became a shared task.

reaction.speaker: Minh
reaction.text: I said no one was chasing An. It sounds funnier when you can actually see An attacking the buttons.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: I think the visual translated perfectly.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I hand the recorder to Jules. For once, I am neither operating the equipment nor narrating the whole room. It is a relief.

scenes.title: A little space

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: Our instructor stops by and asks how the project is developing. I begin explaining why the dinner recording might feel different from an interview.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: “It isn't just a conversation about home. It is...” I stop. I have several possible endings, and none of them feels precise yet.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: Jules is trying to help. But authentic would make it sound as though a planned interview were somehow fake. That is not the distinction I want.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: The instructor waits with a pen resting above her notebook. I do not have to accept the first word offered just to keep the room moving.

scenes.prompt: What do you do with the pause?

note.title: The right to finish a thought
note.text: Word searching also happens in monolingual speech. The scene does not diagnose the cause of An's pause. Offering a word can help, but waiting, checking, and letting the speaker reject a suggestion matter too.

choices.label: “Give me a second. I want to finish the thought.”
choices.detail: Ask for a little more time.
choices.reflection: You asked the room to wait. Your friends learned a small preference about how to support you.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Of course. Sorry, I jumped in.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Thanks. I mean it happens for its own reasons. Dinner isn't happening because we need a project. Recording it changes that a little.”

reaction.speaker: Minh
reaction.text: Let's put that exact sentence in our proposal. It explains why asking first matters.

choices.label: “Close. Help me find a word for something that happens on its own.”
choices.reflection: You welcomed help while keeping control over what you meant.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Unplanned? Or ordinary? Something you would be doing whether we were there or not?

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “That last part.” I write it down. We have not found a perfect single word, but the sentence holds the thought.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: This time the help feels like building something together. I got to say which piece fit.

choices.label: “Let me give you an example instead.”
choices.detail: Explain through a moment, not a label.
choices.reflection: You replaced the missing label with a story. The explanation took longer and made the concern concrete.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “At dinner, Mom asked if we'd eaten. If I ask her to repeat that for a microphone, the words might be identical, but she would be doing something different.”

reaction.speaker: Minh
reaction.text: Right. One is checking on you. The other is showing the class what checking on you sounds like.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: The instructor writes that down. Sometimes an example does the work I was demanding from a single word.
